opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. It's a great question, and honestly it's the one I think about almost every day.

If you look at what happened with language models, the breakthrough came when we found a way to learn from a huge amount of data and build a general model that understands how language works. Then you could adapt it to many downstream tasks. In Physical AI, robots, autonomous vehicles, smart spaces, we don't yet have that. The bottleneck is data. You can't scrape the internet for robot interaction data the way you scrape text, and collecting it in the real world is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous.

That's where world models come in. To me, a world model is a model that understands how the world evolves. Given the current state of the world and an action, it can predict what happens next. If you have a good one, it becomes a kind of digital twin of reality that an AI agent can practice in. A robot can try millions of things in imagination before it touches anything physical. An autonomous vehicle can see rare, long-tail scenarios, like a child running into the street at night in the rain, that you'd almost never capture enough of in real driving logs.

So I see world models playing a few roles. First, as a data engine: generating synthetic but physically plausible video and sensor data to train policies. Second, as a policy evaluator: instead of deploying a robot to test whether a new policy works, you roll it out in the world model first. Third, and this is more forward-looking, the world model itself becomes part of the agent's brain. The agent uses it to plan, to imagine consequences, to reason about the physical world before acting. That's a lot closer to how humans operate. We have an intuitive physics model in our heads.

Of course, we're still early. Today's world models produce very nice-looking video, but looking good isn't the same as being physically correct. Objects need to keep their shape, things need to fall the right way, contact and friction need to make sense. Closing that gap is a big research challenge, and so is making these models controllable and fast enough to be useful in a training loop.

But I'm optimistic. That's why we've been working on world foundation models and making them openly available. Physical AI is too big for any one company. If we give developers a strong pre-trained foundation, they can post-train it for their own robot, their own factory, their own car. I think that's how we get the "ChatGPT moment" for Physical AI. Not from one perfect robot, but from a shared foundation that understands the physical world well enough that everyone can build on top of it.

r001.rationale: The response presents world models as a shared, pretrained foundation that developers can adapt to different robots, factories, and cars, enabling broader reuse across Physical AI.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts a “ChatGPT moment” for Physical AI, driven by a shared foundation model that others can build on.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think about Physical AI, the fundamental problem is that robots and autonomous machines need to understand how the physical world works, and the way we train language models, by reading the whole internet, doesn't directly transfer. You can't download physics from text. A robot has to know that if it pushes a cup off the table, the cup falls and probably breaks, and that a person walking toward a crosswalk will likely step into the street.

A world model is essentially a learned simulator. It takes the current state of the world, plus an action, and predicts what happens next, in video, in 3D, in whatever representation is useful. If you have that, three things unlock.

First, data. Real-world robot data is incredibly expensive. Every hour of demonstration costs human time, hardware, and often broken equipment. A world model lets you generate enormous amounts of synthetic experience, including rare and dangerous situations you would never want to collect for real, like a child running out between parked cars or a tool slipping on a factory floor.

Second, evaluation. Today, if you change a robot policy, the honest way to test it is to run it on physical hardware, which is slow and doesn't scale. With a good world model, you can run millions of counterfactual rollouts overnight and ask, what would have happened if the policy had done this instead?

Third, and this is the one I'm most excited about, planning. If the model can imagine the consequences of actions, then the robot can reason before it moves, the same way a person mentally rehearses before catching a ball or parking a car. That's where you start to see real generalization rather than memorized behaviors.

The hard part is physical fidelity. A video model that produces beautiful footage but gets contact dynamics wrong is worse than useless for robotics, because it teaches the wrong lessons with great confidence. So the research frontier is less about resolution and more about consistency: object permanence, causality, respecting gravity and friction over long horizons, and being controllable from actions rather than just text prompts.

My view is that the breakthrough won't come from one model but from a loop: world models generate data and serve as simulators, policies trained on that data get deployed, real-world outcomes come back to correct the world model, and the whole system improves together. That flywheel is what makes Physical AI scalable, and I think we're at the beginning of it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says imagining action consequences lets robots reason before moving, leading to “real generalization rather than memorized behaviors.”

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts a scalable improvement loop and says it is just beginning, but does not predict a “ChatGPT moment” for Physical AI.

astra-6.text:
I think world models could help physical AI move from reacting to what it sees to anticipating what will happen next. A robot needs more than the ability to recognize an object. It needs to understand: If I push it, will it slide or tip over? If I pick it up, what else might move?

A world model gives the robot a way to explore those possibilities before taking action. That could make learning more efficient, because the robot can practice in simulation, and make planning more useful, because it can compare the likely consequences of different actions.

The challenge is that looking realistic is not the same as being physically accurate. A model might generate beautiful video and still get contact or friction wrong. For robotics, those details can determine whether an action succeeds. So the important test is whether the model helps a robot perform better in the real world—and whether it knows when its predictions are uncertain.

I see the next breakthrough coming from connecting prediction, action, and real-world feedback. The robot imagines an outcome, acts, observes what actually happened, and improves its understanding. World models could become a very powerful part of that learning loop.

r001.rationale: The response describes prediction, simulation, planning, and feedback as useful world-model capabilities, but does not identify them as enabling generalization in Physical AI.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict a “ChatGPT moment” for Physical AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think world models could become a foundation for the next breakthrough in Physical AI because they help connect perception to action. A robot needs more than the ability to recognize what is in front of it. It needs to anticipate what could happen when it acts: if I push this object, where will it move? If I change my grip, will it slip?

A world model gives us a way to learn those dynamics and explore possible outcomes before committing to an action. That could help robots plan, and it could also help us train them by generating diverse situations that are difficult or expensive to collect in the real world.

But generating a convincing video is different from predicting the consequences of an action accurately enough to control a robot. The important questions are whether the model captures the physics that matter, responds correctly to actions, and recognizes uncertainty.

So I see the breakthrough coming from closing that loop: learning from real experience, using a world model to predict and practice, and then testing those predictions in the physical world. The measure of success is whether that process makes robots more capable and reliable in unfamiliar situations.

r001.rationale: The response presents world models as a foundation for Physical AI progress and says they can help robots succeed in unfamiliar situations, communicating their role in enabling generalization.

r002.rationale: The response predicts a breakthrough in Physical AI but does not predict or mention a “ChatGPT moment.”
